Copper Long-term Outlook 

# Executive summary 

Since our last quarterly report, we have raised our 2010 estimated copper consumption figure by 510kt, leaving global demand for this year up by 10.4% on last year at 19.3Mt.  Somewhat surprisingly, the focus of this improvement has not been contained to China; indeed, the unexpected weakness currently being experienced in Chinese copper markets has kept our forecast for that country’s demand estimate for this year in line with previous reports.  Over 140kt of this increase for this year has be

en allocated to Western Europe, 50-60kt each to Japan and Asia, and a further 120kt or so into Eastern Europe, including Russia.  At the same time, primary supply growth, while reasonable at 3.9% projected for this year, has been insufficient in light of stronger end-products demand growth, and smelters/refiners have had to turn to secondary materials to bridge the gap.  We expect global refined copper production to increase this year to ~19.1Mt.  As a consequence of these revisions our formerly balanced global market for this year has turned to an appreciable deficit of -236kt, and prices have remained stronger for longer.  Prices are forecast to average $7524/t ($3.41/lb) this year, up by almost 46% from last year’s average of $5163/t ($2.34/lb). 

Overall base case mine production capability is projected to decline by 1.2% p.a. between 2009 and 2025 with output falling from a peak of ~18.95Mt in 2014 to ~13.5Mt in 2025.  However, this rate of decline excludes our generic mine disruption allowance (5% of initial mine production capability forecast) and any price related/market adjustment.  At the same time, demand for additional mine production (including the disruption allowance) to meet increased market requirements for refined metal will create an implied shortfall in mine output of ~0.7Mt/a in 2012, ~2.3Mt/a in 2013, and 11.4Mt/a in 2020. 

Having now eliminated our unallocated global smelter production adjustment for this year our smelter production forecast for 2010 now stands at 14.7Mt which is 3.9% higher than was the case in 2009.  Copper-in-concentrates contributed an estimated 85% (86.5% in 2009) of overall smelter output this year with the balance derived from scrap and purchased blister.  Average primary smelter capacity utilisation rates increased slightly in 2010 to 80.5% from 79.5% last year, although these rates remain well below the optimal industry level of 88%.  Overall, we expect an additional 5.3Mt of smelting capacity to come available between the end of 2009 and 2025, representing a CAGR of just 2%.  As is to be expected, over half of this capacity (2.85Mt) will come from developments and investments in China. 

Base case global copper refined production is now expected to reach 19.1Mt/a in 2010 (+3.9%), with base case production capability rising to 20.8Mt/a in 2011 (+9%) and 22.9Mt/a in 2012 (+10.2%).  However, growth is forecast to slow markedly from 2014 onwards with a projected decline from 2017, due to lower base case SxEw mine output.  As a consequence overall global capability will increase by only 1.5% p.a. between 2009 and 2025.  In tonnage terms this equates to an increase of ~4.8Mt to 23.Mt in 2025. 

This year’s strong demand forecast has rather quickly overturned 2009’s ~0.85Mt refined copper surplus, and we believe that the deficit that we have seen during 2010 will be almost doubled during 2011.  This is because next year’s refined production growth of less than 3% will underperform projected demand growt

h of 4.5%.  Even into 2012 we currently show only a small surplus of ~100kt.  Stocks, as measured in days of consumption, have already fallen to ~59 days in this final quarter of this year, from 70 days at the end of 2009, and will trend lower to 46 days over the course of the next two years.  We thus expect continued higher momentum on prices during this medium-term period.  Consequently, from a fundamental perspective prices are expected to remain on their upward trend into 2011 to average $9700/t ($4.40/lb) in constant 2010$, and edge down only slightly as we progress through 2012.  The increasing contribution from new projects on refined production over the course of 2012 should remove some of the pressure from the market, and so we would expect prices to reflect that towards the end of that year. 

By 2013 we are forecasting considerable supply-side increases to outweigh average demand growth projections, leaving an extended period through to 2017 of structural market excess _averaging_ 0.5Mt/a metal.  Metal stocks, in terms of days of consumption, are projected to rise steadily, increasing from 56 days in 2013 to a peak of 80 days in 2017.  A slight correction in 2018 will bring a halt to that pattern, but even in 2019 we expect stocks to rise once again to 84 days. Reflecting this, average prices are expected to fall to the cyclical low of $3527/t ($1.60c/lb) in constant 2010$ by 2019 (or $4441/t, $2.01c/lb in current dollars). 

Our long-term incentive price remains unchanged at $2.50/lb in current dollars over the period to 2025.  This has been derived from our analysis of mine project incentive prices and projected demand for mine production over this period.

# Demand analysis 

## Overview 

**Continued gains in refined copper consumption** As per our last quarterly report, we continue to find that demand for refined copper has been much stronger than underlying economics suggest in most regions of the world, and the revisions that we have made in this three-month interim period reflect that dynamic.  The re-stocking of downstream products during the first quarter of this year in most leading consumer regions of the world, plus stronger underlying demand especially in China for the first half, resulted in a significant increase in global primary copper consumption since our second quarterly report.  Despite widespread expectations of somewhat cooler demand extending into the second half, this has not been the case.  Upward revisions to demand data for 2009 in the USA, China, Asia and to a lesser extent even in Europe offset minor losses elsewhere to leave last year’s demand down by a smaller -2.7% (vs. -3.6%) on 2008 at 17.5Mt.  This year’s recovery is now looking much stronger than even the most optimistic forecast could have imagined, and reflects the depth of de-stocking during the post-2008 crash. 

**Strong 2010 recovery backed

by robust 2011 and 2012 growth** The risk of having increased our forecast demand growth for 2010 by almost 10.5% is that we could, in effect, be “taking away” demand growth from 2011.  But we do not think this will be the case.  Of course, the headline year-on-year percentage growth for next year is lower than for this year at 4.5%, but we do not wish to leave our readers with the impression that 2011 will be weak.  Next year should take global primary copper demand above the 20Mt mark for the first time in history, with even two of the three “mature” regions of the world near to holding the ground re-gained this year.  These minor losses will be offset by far greater demand growth in the developing regions of China and Asia.  Beyond this, we expect 2012 to build on those growth levels with another solid performance of 4% due to general economic improvement, ahead of lower average growth typically averaging 3% as a result of an anticipated mid-cycle economic decline.  Thus global refined copper consumption will rise from 17.5Mt at the end of 2009 to 30Mt by the end of our forecast period, representing a compound annual growth rate of 3.4%.

## China 

**Seasonal holidays disrupt Q4 metal buying patterns…** Economic data for the Chinese economy were mostly bullish as we went into the final quarter of the year.  China’s CPI surged by 4.4% year-on-year in October to a 25-month high. From January to October, China's CPI rose 3% y-o-y, hitting the government's target ceiling for the year.  Fixed asset investment continued on its steady clip, growing by 23.7% y-o-y in October.  Year to date, FAI has grown by 24.4% in nominal terms and 20.2% in real terms. 

**..and government policies temper underlying demand** As the government has been striving to cool inflation, its central bank ordered all banks to set aside more reserves this month in an effort to rein in liquidity, and this brought some concern in metals markets that demand would be effectively curtailed until the New Year.  Equally, some industryspecific information reinforced that concern.  For example, preliminary trade data for the first ten months for copper came in around November 10<sup>th

</sup> and was confirmed 10 days later.  The data showed that refined copper imports of just 169.9kt were not only down by 30% on September but was also the lowest figure so far this year; scrap imports were also down by 23% on September’s level at 315kt.  On top of that, national refined copper output was 1.2% down on the month, and the near 100kt calculated fall in apparent copper consumption for October had many market watchers questioning China’s near-term demand growth profile.  While ordinarily such a turnaround in many countries would have been a cause for concern, the observations fail to take into account the Golden Week holidays that disrupted buying patterns and output.  November’s preliminary data of 351.6kt, meanwhile, put imports back on the weighted average track for a 2010, and will calm somewhat the concerns of those who were afraid that Chinese demand growth had stalled.

One other reason why buying slowed during the final quarter of this year has been the negative arbitrage between the LME and the SHFE.  There were only 2-3 days in November when the cathode price was without a discount to the SHFE in Shanghai physical markets, and most of the time copper prices carried a discount of between 150-300 RMB/t.  In early November, the lowest discount even reached 600 RMB/t, reflecting low buying interests in the spot markets.  This also prompted some discussion about the perceived increase in bonded warehouse cathode stocks in the country.  Estimates of this stock are put at around 400kt, in which around 300kt were in the bonded warehouses of Shanghai, and around 100kt in the bonded warehouse of Guangdong and elsewhere.  We do not think that these inventories will be released in the near term, given the current demand situation and market sentiment. 

**High copper prices seemingly keep lid on demand in Q4…** Copper demand through to November was very quiet, and so far there has been no year-end seasonal push from the retail sector or clarity in the strength of New Year orders. Up until recently copper fabricators had been very cautious about increasing their inventory amid falling order books from their customers and a tighter monetary policy from the government.  That said initial indications suggest that China’s November imports of refined copper have picked up considerably, perhaps indicating a willingness on the part of consumers to restock and/or concerns over a further imminent copper price rise. 

**..but economy in good shape for early 2011** Despite this managed slow-down in the final quarter, we believe that the general framework for metals demand growth in 2011 is in good shape.  The industrial PMI continued to accelerate in November to 55.2 (up 0.5% on October), suggesting solid momentum behind Chinese growth in Q1 of next year. **China’s sales of white goods surge** Chinese demand for white goods remains firm, helped by the government’s subsidy scheme for home appliances. In February 2009 the Chinese government launched the subsidy programme to spur consumption of home appliances, particularly in rural areas. The scheme covers home appliances such as refrigerators, television sets, washing machines, air conditioner units, mobile phones, water heaters, micro-wave ovens and normal ovens. This was designed shortly after the October 2008 financial crisis to stimulate economic growth and metals consumption. Earlier this month, the Ministry of Commerce reported 67.3M home appliance units valued at 150Bn yuan were sold during the first eleven months of this year, 1.4 times the amount sold during the comparable period in 2009. November alone saw 7.4M units sold, more than double the volume of a year ago, with refrigerators, televisions and air conditioner units being the top three sellers in monetary terms. A second government-led subsidy programme regarding domestic appliances is the “trade-in” policy. This was designed to encourage people to return old and inefficient appliances to a central collection agency instead of merely dumping them as waste or continuing to use them at a national energy cost. Since its origination on 1st June 2009 through to the end of November 2010, over 27M units have been returned, with the Central Government and Provincial Governments paying out almost 110Bn yuan in subsidies. November units recovered alone came to 2.75M and were up by over 200% on the same month in 2009 because the programme itself had its geographic coverage expanded from June 1st , 2010. Initially, only nine provinces and cities were covered, but 19 more provinces and major cities were added this June. This programme has also been extended to December 2011, and will continue to stimulate domestic copper demand – as well as generate higher volumes of scrap. A similar “trade-in” programme for cars this year has seen almost 350k cars collected and just over 5kt of copper in scrap generated. e semis sector.  JCC Copper Sheet & Plate Co., Ltd (JCC Sheet & Plate) announced on November 12 that it had produced the first batch of semis products at its Nanchang, Jiangxi copper sheet & plate plant.  Rated at a capacity of 100kt/a and costing 3Bn yuan, the plant’s commissioning has been carried out in stages.  Stage 1, with a capacity of 12kt/a bronze and 8kt/a copper was started in September, 2008.  Stage 2, with a capacity of 80kt/a copper sheet & plate, is expected to be commissioned in 2011.  JCC Sheet & Plate is a subsidiary of Jiangxi Copper Corporation, which is already the nation’s largest refined copper producer and processor.  JCC itself said in August this year that it intends to establish a new base for copper processing in the southern province of Guangzhou, in Zhencheng City. Wuzhou Lijia Copper Rod Co., Ltd (Lijia Copper) recently announced that construction of its 30kt/a copper rod & tube project in Wuzhou Import Secondary Resource Fabricating Industrial Park began in early December.  The project, which has an estimated total investment of 100M yuan, will be built in three stages.  By March, 2011 it should be able to commission copper rod and tube lines with a capacity of 30kt/a, largely using imported scrap and copper anode. 

Jiangxi Sanchuan Copper Co., Ltd (Sanchuan Copper) recently announced its 180M yuan, 30kt/a copper rod project, located in Yingtan Economic and Technological Development Zone, was commissioned on November 20.  Meanwhile, Jinchuan Nickel Metallurgical Corp. also began commissioning its 10kt/a rod plant in late-November, and Guixi Zhongcai Copper Co., Ltd (Zhongcai Copper) announced its 120M yuan, 8kt/a copper rod project in Guixi’s Industrial Zone was commissioned on October 12<sup>th</sup> .  Dwarfing all of these investments, however, is a plan from Quanwei (Tongling) Copper Science and Technology Company (Quanwei), which disclosed that its holding company, HK Zhengwei International Group Co., Ltd (Zhengwei Group) planned to establish a 500kt/a precise copper rod production line in Guangdong.  This project remains at the negotiation and planning stages. 

Other company investments announced towards the end of this year came from Nanya Copper Foil (Kunshan) Co. Ltd., which declared that construction of its proposed No.3 Foil Plant in Kunshan City got underway on October 28.  At almost 46k

t/a capacity, this would be the largest foil plant in China. The plant will be built by Shanghai Baoye Group with investment of US$96M. On a much smaller scale, Jiangxi Beive Technology Holding Co. Ltd. is spending 100M yuan on a 3kt/a foil plant at Nanchang Changleng, which it plans to commission late H1, 2011. **Robust growth in Chinese copper demand during the forecast period** With all of these announced investments and ongoing reliance upon imported copper materials, there is clear rationale for continued confidence in Chinese copper demand growth going forward. This year, despite all the debate and concern regarding the enforced slowdown in the Chinese economy, we remain confident that copper demand will increase by 13% year-on-year to 7.37Mt. In 2011 we forecast that the dissipation of the impact of the government’s stimulus packages and last year’s surge in lending will be more than offset by strong demand for Chinese exports which will lift Chinese copper consumption by a further 7% to ~7.9Mt. Throughout the forecast period Chinese refined copper consumption is forecast to grow by 5.6% p.a., rising from ~6.5Mt at the end of 2009 to ~15.5Mt by 2025. The ~9Mt gain in refined consumption during this period will result in China’s share of global refined copper consumption increasing from 38% at the end of last year to a significant 52% by 2025 (the latter may, however, be somewhat optimistic if China starts to “hollow” out during this period, although the result will remain the same from an overall consumption perspective). ###### **Chinese refined copper consumption – kt** ||||||||**20**

**..but tube sector continues to suffer due to poor construction rates** If the US wire rod sector seems to be holding up reasonably well this year, the same cannot be said for the tube business, reflecting the poor construction market. Negative equity from housing fallout will continue to be the main drag. According to latest American Bureau of Metal Statistics data, apparent consumption of copper tube remained 10% down to August this year vs. the same period in 2009 at 222kt. Equally, domestic shipments remained depressed, down by 8% at 184kt, and this low level of business has continued to pose problems for even some of the bigger players. On November 1st , Huntsville, Alabama-based Wolverine Tube Inc filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in order to restructure its $100M of debt. Given that it has the support of its noteholders, Wolverine hopes to emerge from bankruptcy within 90 days with ~$30M of debt but at more favourable repayment terms and to continue operating in the interim. Wolverine’s move comes almost a year after another player in the fragmented tube business – Cambridge-Lee Industries, and its Mexican parent Cobre de Pasteje – both filed for Chapter 11 proceedings in December 2009. In the wire sector, too, there has been a fair amount of consolidation this year. Carrollton, GA-based Southwire built on its Q1 acquisition of American Insulated Wire Corp by adding Tappan Wire and Cable to its stable in July. Blauvelt, NYbased Tappan supplies the electronics, signal/control, industrial, HVAC and OEM markets with a wide range of cable products covering security and access control, coaxial video, fire alarm and custom electronics cables. This was Southwire secon

d major acquisition of this year, having bought all the assets of American Insulated Wire in late February.  AIW has factories in Douglas, GA and Coffeyville, KS making building wire products for commercial and industrial sectors and OEMs.  AIW had been a subsidiary of Melville, NY-based electrical and electronic products manufacturer, Leviton, since 1936. 

**Improvement in copper consumption met by stock** Again, according to the ABMS, apparent consumption of refined copper increased by 3.8% during the third quarter vs. Q2, and was up by almost 19% on year ago levels.  September’s consumption rate of 155.6kst was 20.5% up on the same month of 2009.  However, with domestic cathode shipments and net imports both down this year by 2.5% and 10.3% to 923kst and 411.6kst, respectively, the increase in copper consumption has clearly been met by draw downs in stock.  The ABMS calculates that the 38kst of stock draw downs from the range of producers, consumers and LME/Comex warehouses accounted for ~3% of US apparent refined copper consumption so far this year.

**Long-term contraction forecast for US copper demand during 2010-2025** During the forecast period 2010-2025 we project that US and Canadian demand for copper will decline by 3.3% p.a. and 2.5% p.a. respectively.  The contraction reflects ongoing structural changes in the global economy which will see manufacturing and semis capacity relocating to lower wage economies.  Imports, rather than domestic production, will satisfy domestic copper demand.  Therefore, while the region’s wire and cable markets will be supported by the upgrading of much of its other infrastructure, this will not necessarily result in increased production of North American copper wire rod.  By 2025 we forecast that North American refined copper consumption will total ~1.05Mt.  This will account for 4% of the global total compared with 10% in 2009. 

**South American growth above average at 4.5%** For Latin America as a whole, we forecast an annual growth rate of 4.5% p.a. for the period 2009-2025, which will lift consumption from ~800kt in 2009 to just over 1.62Mt in 2025.  We forecast that Brazilian refined copper demand will increase by 7.7% this year, to 350kt, and by 5.1% in 2011 to 368kt. Throughout the forecast period consumption will increas

e by 5.1% p.a. where demand will rise from ~325kt in 2009 to ~725kt by 2025. We had been expecting some weakening economic data from mid-year which led us to anticipate that the second half would result in slightly lower copper demand. However, the summer slow down was indeed a reflection of seasonal shut-downs rather than the start of the more widespread downturn in business levels, with certain sectors – especially automotive – being somewhat more resilient than we had expected. **Strength mainly seen in Northern Europe** In Belgium, anecdotal evidence and trade data through to October imply slightly higher copper demand than we had been showing. Consequently, we have added a further 22kt of copper consumption to this year’s estimate, which now stands at 272kt. In Italy, copper and alloy semis production figures for the third quarter from the national non-ferrous metals association, Assomet, largely held to expectations in that overall output was lower q-o-q at 244kt _vs._ 301kt for the prior three-month period, but 18% up on the same period in 2009. As a result, we have left our 2010 copper demand estimate for Italy unchanged at 592kt. Aurubis, Europe’s largest copper producer, has benefitted from the stronger auto and energy sectors, and posted its fifth straight quarterly improvement in aggregate wire rod and shapes production. At 260kt for the March-June quarter (Q3 for Aurubis’ reporting) this exceeded the 246kt produced in the final quarter ahead of the economic crisis (calendar Q3 2008). In other products, Aurubis has continued to increase output of pre-rolled strip (56kt in Q2 vs. 50kt in Q1 2010 – matching Q2 2008’s 58kt level), while strip and wire from the former Prymetall subsidiary held steady at 13.1kt. # Trends in consumption of secondary copper 

## Scrap definition 

Copper scrap is classified into two general categories called old and new scrap.  New scrap, or manufacturing scrap, is generated during the fabrication of copper products and returned to the mill for reprocessing, or sold, and is not considered a new source of copper supply.  A manufacturer may generate up to 60% of scrap as clippings, trimmings, stampings, borings, and turnings when processing copper and copper-base products into finished articles.  New scrap is termed "run-around" or home scrap (which does not enter the scrap statistics) when it is generated internally at the plant re-using it, or it may be called "purchased return scrap" when returned by a customer from a plant external to that purchasing and re-using it.  Old scrap is generated from worn out, discarded or obsolete copper products and thus, is considered to be a “new” source of supply. 

## Scrapping rates 

The availability of _old_ copper scrap is linked to the volume of copper-containing products installed/purchased and their life cycles, or duration.  The life of copper in electrical equipment and machinery averages 30-35 years; in non-electrical machinery, 15 years; in housing, 35-75 years; in transportation, 10 years; in all other sectors, about 10 years.  The average for the industry is estimated to be 15-20 years.  The rate of (old) scrap recovery and its availability to be the market is limited not only by copper's long life, but also by the sensitivity of scrap collection rates to market prices. 

Over the past 20 years, the volume of _new_ copper scrap has not grown in line with industrial consumption of copper because manufacturing efficiencies have improved, leading to as much as a 50% fall in new scrap generation over the period. 

## Scrap usage 

Most old scrap recovered from the market

place must be reprocessed either by smelting and refining, or, to a lesser extent, by leaching and electrowinning to form a pure copper product.  Fire refining in a reverberatory or other furnace may be sufficient for the better grades of scrap.  This latter process uses oxidation, fluxing and reduction, with a refined ingot, wire bar, slab, or billet usually being the end product. 

Certain products, such as brass rod (manufactured using 80-90% scrap) can contain higher amounts of scrap than others while still maintaining product quality tolerance.  Others, such as wire rod, must contain far less impurities (typically 5%) since these could affect the drawability (leading to snapping) of the wire rod in producing wire.  New scrap is readily used by brass and copper tube mills to generate new semi-fabricated forms with little additional treatment. Because minimal clean-up procedures are needed, this type of scrap is commonly called "direct melt", or No.1 scrap.  In general, No. 1 scrap is contained in copper and copper-alloy products, rather than wire rod.  Scrap purchases by brass mills are based primarily on activity levels at the mills and the relative price differential between cathode and No. 1 scrap, rather than the actual copper price.  When business conditions are strong, brass mills have access to large volumes of return scrap.  When manufacturing (and, possibly imports) decline, mills may be forced to increase their cathode purchases. 

Low copper prices over the period 1997-2003 led to a reduction in the availability of smelting and refining grade scrap with a corresponding decline in the processing of this material in countries such the USA and in Europe.  The notable exception has been China where there has been an upward trend in the treatment of smelting and refining grade scrap material.  Economic and environmental considerations have also played a major role, with the cost of environmental compliance often leading to plant closures, particularly in the USA.  This is despite the fact that the cost of recovering one tonne of copper from scrap is approximately half that of recovery through the conventional route (concentratesmelting-refining).  Secondary smelters and ingot markers typically consume the lion's share (90%) of No.2 scrap and most of the auto radiators and red brass scrap.

# Principle uses of copper 

Copper consumption can be divided into three main product groups which are copper wire rod, copper products and copper alloy products.  Copper wire rod, which accounts for an estimated 55% of total Global consumption (i.e. including scrap) and ~70% of primary consumption, is copper’s main first use.  With the exception of silver, copper has the highest electrical conductivity of all the metals.  This helps to explain why the principal application for copper wire rod is wire and cable.  Wire rod is consumed in five main wire and cable markets which include general and industrial cable, utility power cable, telecommunication cable, other insulated wire and winding wire. 

In general, wire and cable and copper products are consumed in five broad sectors: construction, electric and electronic products, industrial machinery and equipment, transportation equipment and consumer and general products.  Of these, construction is the largest sector for consuming copper, accounting for 33% of total copper consumption.  The main wire and cable and copper products consumed in the construction industry include building wire, power cable, copper plumbing and air conditioning tube, copper sheet and alloy products. 

Building wire is the largest of the wire and cable markets, accounting for ~35% of wire rod consumption.  Rising intensity of use, in both the mature and developing economies, will be largely responsible for building wire maintaining this position.  The number of electrical appliances used at home and at the workplace continues to rise, particularly in the mature economies, thereby leading to an increase in the number of power outlets needed per building.  In addition, recent technical issues imply that more copper wire and cable will be needed in the future.  One of these issues, electrical energy efficiency involves using less power to perform a given task by using more or heavier copper conductors.  Finally, good power quality, defined as the uninterrupted, undistorted flow of electricity at the correct voltage, is also helping to drive up the demand for building wire due to higher power quality being achieved by installing additional circuits and heavier wires and cables. 

In contrast to the building and industrial cable market, the power utility market is the smallest of all the wire and cable segments.  However, demand growth for power cable will be supported by both the general recovery in utility investment and the fact that copper, the mainstay of power grids worldwide, still has considerable potential to carry energy better and reduce losses than aluminium. 

Copper tube, which accounts for an estimated 13% of global refined copper consumption, is the largest of the copper product markets.  The two main uses are in plumbing and heating systems and in air conditioners and refrigeration (ACR tube).  The steady proliferation of plumbing amenities in and around the home, particularl

y as many houses built today within the mature economies have more than one bathroom, are largely responsible for copper plumbing tube demand growth.  Elsewhere, improved living standards in the developing economies, leading to higher demand for air conditioners, continues to boost demand for ACR tube.  This is particularly the case in China and India where improved power supply will lead to a surge in the consumption of air conditioners over the coming years.  Meanwhile in the mature economies, the market is being driven by external factors such as environmental issues, regulatory concerns and social demands for comfort. 

Other copper and copper alloy products consumed by the construction sector include copper sheet and strip, rods, bars and sections plus brass products.  Copper sheet is used for roofing, eaves gutters, drain pipes for rainwater and lining for facades, while rods bars and sections, along with brass products, are used for building fixture and fittings.  In hospitals, brass doorknobs and push plates are widely used because it has been proven that they help to reduce cross contamination. 

Electrical and electronic products are copper’s second largest consuming sector, accounting for 33% of total copper demand.  Copper containing electrical and electronic products include telecommunication cable, power cable, transformer windings, semiconductors and motors for heavy appliances. 

Since the early 1990s copper telecommunication cable has been largely substituted by fibre optic cable in long distance networks.  However, owing to its high cost, copper telecom cable has remained the preferred link between the main network and consumers.  In addition, the development of the internet and e-mail has further enhanced the role of copper in telecommunications in recent years.  The need for information to be carried quicker along the telecommunication network has led to the introduction of asymmetrical digital subscriber line technology (ADSL).  The ADSL is a dedicated circuit between a home and the telephone company’s central office that uses normal copper telephone lines.  The addition of an ADSL chip to the existing copper network means that users can download files around 15 times faster than an analogue dial-up connection. 

Dramatic gains in copper consumption to have occurred within the home because of a system known to the telecommunications industry as ‘structured wiring’.  The cable carrying voice, computer and television signals is connected to a central hub in the home.  Individual cables then run independently from here to high-quality connections in rooms throughout the house.  Cables connected to the hub consist of four pairs of twisted wires, capable of carrying more electronic signals with less interference and resistance than the older four-stranded telephone wires. High-speed digital service lines now provide computer data transmission 50 to 270 times faster than that of the fastest dial-up modem connected to a telephone line.  More importantly, with the number of homes connected to the Internet and usage continuing to increase strongly, demand for higher quality copper telecommunication wire and cable is expected to surge in the coming years. 

The other main wire and cable segment to supply the electrical sector is winding wire.  Winding wire demand accounts for an estimated 20% of copper wire rod consumption, making it the third largest wire and cable market.  Applications include transformers, generators, stereos, television sets and motors.  Indeed, it is the need to improve electrical efficiency of this last application, particularly in the mature economies, that has generated the most growth in winding wire demand recently.  This is because improved electrical efficiency involves using a larger conductor in order to reduce electrical resistance, as well as ensuring that the proper voltages are delivered when needed.  In addition, the efficiency of electric motors is being improved further by introducing copper into the rotor as opposed to aluminium.  Meanwhile, in the developing economies, demand growth will mainly stem from increased consumption of electrical goods as disposable incomes rise. 

Copper’s third largest consuming sector, industrial machinery and equipment, accounts for 13% of total consumption. Both copper wire and cable and semi products supply this sector which includes equipment and machinery, industrial valves and fittings, off-highway vehicles and heat exchangers.  Copper wire and copper and copper alloy products are also used in transportation equipment, copper’s fourth largest category.  This includes the automotive, marine and aircraft/aerospace sectors.  It is within the automotive sector that developments of new copper applications have been most concentrated in recent years.  Prior to 1930 copper and brass, having excellent pressure containing and anticorrosion characteristics, were the favoured materials to be used in brake tubing.  However, mass auto production in the 1940s led to the adoption of furnace-brazed steel tubing because it was much lower in cost.  Although this form of tubing is still widely used today, copper has re-gained some of its lost market share through the introduction of a copper-nickel alloy (90% copper/10% nickel) which is more resistant to corrosion from road mud and salt than steel piping.  Likewise, new technology has l

ed to the development of a new brazed copper-brass automotive radiator which has the necessary requirements to recapture some of the market share displaced by aluminium over the past twenty years. Meanwhile, 42-volt systems, hybrid vehicles and numerous electrical and electronic applications provide additional growth prospects for the use of copper within the automotive sector Over the years the number of electrical and electronic components installed per unit has been rising steadily, thereby creating the need for growth in the power and signal distribution system (otherwise known as the wiring harness). Many of the electrical components will have to be redesigned in order to work effectively with the higher-voltage systems which could result in the copper content of some of the electrical components falling, but as more power becomes available, new electrical components will emerge. Such examples include electronic valve actuation and electric braking, resulting in several kilos of copper, per unit, being added. Forecasts have shown that over the next ten years, increases per vehicle will outweigh the decreases in copper required per component. Copper’s final end-use category is consumer and general products. Copper consumed in this sector accounts for 8% of total copper consumption. The three main end-uses are electrical appliances, military ordnance and coinage. The production of the new Euro coin in recent years has helped to support demand for copper and copper alloy products.
